triage.name: Peripheral Arterial Disease
triage.reason: Common atherosclerotic disease presenting with intermittent claudication; diagnosis reachable by history, vascular exam and ankle-brachial index, with clear risk-factor counseling.

review_issues: exam: term 'Prolonged capillary refill' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Calf tenderness' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Skin warmth' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: More common in older adults, with prevalence rising sharply after age 60
More common in men than women, especially before age 70
Higher prevalence in people who smoke, have diabetes, or have chronic kidney disease
family_history: First-degree relative with peripheral arterial disease
First-degree relative with coronary artery disease

chief_complaints.text: My legs cramp up when I walk and stop when I rest

hpi.onset: Gradual, over months to years; often first noticed when walking farther or faster
hpi.duration: Weeks to months at presentation; symptoms are usually stable or slowly worsening
hpi.progression: Pain comes on after a predictable walking distance, resolves within minutes of rest, and returns with the same amount of effort; over time the pain may appear at shorter distances or occur at rest if severe
hpi.location: Calf most often; may involve the thigh, hip, or buttock if the iliac arteries are narrowed
hpi.radiation: Usually none; may be felt as an aching that spreads upward from the calf
hpi.quality: Cramping, aching, heaviness, fatigue, or numbness in the leg muscles
hpi.severity: Moderate enough to force stopping; often 4–7/10 during walking, then resolves
hpi.timing: Only with exertion; absent at rest unless critical limb ischemia has developed
aggravating: Walking faster or carrying heavy objects
relieving: Standing still for a few minutes

associated_symptoms.text: Leg feels numb or weak during walking
Trouble getting or keeping an erection
Foot pain at night that improves when hanging the leg down
Nonhealing sore on the foot or toe

pertinent_negatives: Back pain radiating down both legs
Leg swelling or calf tenderness after immobility
Fever or warmth over the leg
Color changes of the fingers triggered by cold
Pain that is unchanged by activity or worse with joint movement

positives.text: Leg pain or cramping with walking
Legs feel heavy or tired after walking

argues_against: Pain reproduced by palpation or joint movement

positives.text: Shiny or thin skin on the lower legs

negatives: Back pain that shoots down the leg
argues_against: Bilateral radicular leg pain with prolonged standing

positives.text: Trouble getting or keeping an erection

atypical.how_it_differs: Neuropathy may blunt the typical exertional pain, so patients may present instead with a painless foot ulcer, rest pain, or gangrene without much prior claudication.
They may attribute the pain to aging or have limited walking from other conditions, so classic claudication may be absent or unrecognized until tissue loss or rest pain develops.
missing_classic_features: Pain that forces them to stop walking

atypical.how_it_differs: Decreased mobility may hide exertional leg pain, and discomfort may be localized to the hips or thighs rather than the calves.
missing_classic_features: Calf claudication with a clear walking limit

general.mild: Comfortable at rest; appears well, walks with a normal gait for short distances.
general.moderate: Comfortable at rest; may limp or stop after walking a fixed distance because of claudication.
general.severe: May appear uncomfortable at rest if rest pain is present; may keep the leg hanging down or rub the foot.
general.critical: Ill-appearing if gangrene or infected ulcer is present; may be pale, diaphoretic, or show signs of sepsis.

findings.maneuver: Palpate dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally.
Auscultate over the femoral arteries in the groin.
Feel the dorsum of the foot and compare with the other side.
findings.finding: Cool foot or lower leg compared with the other side

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin of the lower legs and feet.
Elevate the leg to about 60 degrees for 1 minute.
Lower the leg from an elevated position and observe the foot.
findings.finding: Foot becomes dusky red or purple when dependent

findings.maneuver: Press the nail bed of the great toe and release.

findings.finding: Ischemic ulcer, dry gangrene, or tissue loss
No calf tenderness or cord suggesting deep vein thrombosis

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the knee and ankle joints.
findings.finding: No joint effusion, warmth, or tenderness suggesting arthritis

findings.maneuver: Feel the skin over the lower legs.
findings.finding: No warmth or erythema suggesting cellulitis

findings.maneuver: Test lower-extremity strength, sensation, and reflexes.
findings.finding: No motor weakness, sensory loss, or reflex asymmetry suggesting neurogenic claudication

imaging.study: Duplex ultrasound of the lower extremity arteries
imaging.preferred_when: Initial imaging choice for PAD; avoids radiation and iodinated contrast

findings.text: Stenosis or occlusion in femoropopliteal or tibial arteries
Monophasic or dampened distal Doppler waveforms
Visible atherosclerotic plaque with narrowed lumen
Noncompressible, heavily calcified vessel segment limiting assessment

imaging.study: CT angiography of the lower extremities
imaging.preferred_when: Anatomic mapping before revascularization or when duplex is nondiagnostic

imaging.study: MR angiography of the lower extremities
imaging.preferred_when: Contrast allergy or renal impairment when noncontrast time-of-flight technique is used

imaging.study: Catheter angiography of the lower extremities
imaging.preferred_when: Invasive gold standard; usually performed when endovascular intervention is planned

findings.text: Precise focal stenosis or occlusion with runoff assessment

imaging.study: Plain radiograph of the lower extremities

initial.why: First-line noninvasive test to screen for and diagnose PAD; ABI ≤ 0.90 confirms PAD.
Fasting lipid profile to identify and manage dyslipidemia.
Screen for diabetes as a major risk factor.
Assess renal function before contrast imaging or revascularization.

confirmatory.test: Duplex ultrasound of the lower extremity arteries
confirmatory.why: Confirms the location and severity of arterial stenosis without radiation.

supporting.test: CT angiography of the lower extremities
supporting.why: Provides detailed anatomy for revascularization planning.
supporting.only_if: revascularization is being considered or duplex is nondiagnostic

supporting.test: MR angiography of the lower extremities
supporting.why: Alternative to CT angiography when contrast is contraindicated.
supporting.only_if: contrast allergy or severe renal impairment and revascularization planning

supporting.test: Catheter angiography of the lower extremities
supporting.why: Invasive gold standard for precise anatomy.
Useful when ABI is falsely elevated due to noncompressible vessels.
Helps localize the level of stenosis.
supporting.only_if: ABI abnormal and localization needed before revascularization

not_indicated.test: Plain radiograph of the lower extremities
not_indicated.why: Shows only calcification and does not diagnose PAD.
No role in evaluating chronic peripheral arterial disease.

not_indicated.test: Venous duplex ultrasound of the lower extremities
not_indicated.why: Not indicated unless venous obstruction is suspected.

decision_points: Check ABI before and after exercise if resting ABI is normal but symptoms strongly suggest PAD.
Pregnancy test before CT angiography in anyone who could be pregnant.
Avoid gadolinium in severe renal impairment if MR angiography is considered.
Evaluate for critical limb ischemia if rest pain, nonhealing ulcer, or gangrene is present.

criteria.name: Ankle-brachial index diagnostic threshold
criteria.summary: ABI ≤ 0.90 at rest indicates PAD; values 0.91–0.99 are borderline; ABI > 1.40 suggests noncompressible vessels.
items: ABI measured with Doppler in both arms and ankles

differential.name: Acute limb ischemia
differential.why_considered: Sudden severe leg pain with a cold, pulseless limb can mimic severe PAD
differential.trigger: Sudden onset leg pain plus absent pulses, pallor, or neurologic deficits in the leg

history: Sudden onset over minutes to hours, not chronic exertional pain
History of atrial fibrillation, recent myocardial infarction, or arterial embolism
Known peripheral arterial disease with abrupt worsening of symptoms
imaging: CT angiography may show arterial occlusion
ecg: Atrial fibrillation or acute myocardial infarction as an embolic source

differential.name: Deep vein thrombosis
differential.why_considered: Unilateral leg pain, swelling, and heaviness can suggest vascular disease
differential.trigger: Unilateral leg swelling with calf tenderness and risk factors for thrombosis

history: Acute or subacute unilateral leg swelling
Risk factors: recent surgery, immobility, cancer, estrogen use
Pain is constant, not relieved by rest

differential.name: Neurogenic claudication
differential.why_considered: Bilateral leg pain with walking that improves with rest resembles PAD claudication

history: Pain better with leaning forward or sitting, worse with standing upright
Bilateral buttock, thigh, or calf numbness or weakness
Symptoms may improve when walking uphill
exam: Symptoms reproduced by prolonged standing or lumbar extension
imaging: Lumbar spine MRI shows central canal or foraminal stenosis

differential.name: Chronic venous insufficiency
differential.why_considered: Leg heaviness, aching, and skin changes can suggest vascular disease

history: Leg heaviness or aching worsened by prolonged standing
Often worse at end of day
exam: Venous stasis ulcers over medial malleolus
imaging: Venous duplex shows reflux or obstruction

differential.name: Peripheral neuropathy
differential.why_considered: Foot numbness, burning, or pain can be mistaken for PAD

history: Often with history of diabetes, alcohol use, or B12 deficiency
exam: Decreased sensation to monofilament or vibration
Pulses may be normal or diminished due to coexisting PAD
labs: May check HbA1c, B12, or TSH if neuropathy suspected

severity.mild: Asymptomatic or mild claudication only after walking more than 400 meters; ABI 0.70 to 0.90. May not seek care.
severity.moderate: Claudication after 100 to 400 meters, causing predictable stops; pulses and skin findings often mildly reduced but no rest pain or tissue loss.
severity.severe: Rest pain, usually in the forefoot or toes, worse at night and improved by hanging the foot; ABI often below 0.40; no tissue loss yet.
severity.critical: Critical limb ischemia with ischemic rest pain, nonhealing ulcer, or gangrene; imminent limb loss or sepsis from infected gangrene.

red_flags.finding: Sudden onset leg pain with pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paresthesia, or paralysis
red_flags.meaning: Acute limb ischemia; immediate vascular evaluation needed

red_flags.finding: Rest pain or night pain in the foot
red_flags.meaning: Critical limb ischemia; urgent assessment and revascularization
Critical limb ischemia with infection and amputation risk

red_flags.finding: Fever, hypotension, or malodorous drainage from a foot ulcer
ABI greater than 1.40 in a patient with suspected PAD
red_flags.meaning: Noncompressible vessels; need toe pressures or alternative imaging

complications.name: Acute limb ischemia
clues: Embolic source on ECG or history

special_populations.differences: Neuropathy may mask claudication, so patients may present with painless foot ulcers, rest pain, or gangrene without typical exertional pain. Medial calcification can falsely elevate ABI, so toe-brachial index is often needed.

Symptoms may be attributed to aging or limited by reduced mobility, so classic claudication may be absent or unrecognized until rest pain or tissue loss develops. They also have more severe diffuse disease at diagnosis.

Higher prevalence of PAD and more severe arterial calcification. Contrast for CT angiography is riskier, so duplex ultrasound or noncontrast MR angiography may be preferred, and toe pressures can help when ABI is unreliable.

key_questions.question: When you walk, where do you feel the pain or cramping?
key_questions.looking_for: Calf, thigh, or buttock muscle discomfort brought on by exertion

key_questions.question: How far can you walk before it starts, and is it the same distance each time?
key_questions.looking_for: Predictable walking distance; worse with hills or faster pace

key_questions.question: What happens to the pain when you stop and rest?
key_questions.looking_for: Relief within minutes of standing still

key_questions.question: Does the pain ever wake you at night or happen when you are sitting still?
key_questions.looking_for: Rest pain or night pain; suggests critical limb ischemia

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any sores or wounds on your feet or toes that are not healing?
key_questions.looking_for: Nonhealing ulcer or gangrene; critical limb ischemia

key_questions.question: Have you ever had sudden severe leg pain with a cold, pale, or numb leg?
Do you smoke or have you smoked cigarettes in the past?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or former smoking; strongest modifiable risk factor

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, or kidney disease?
Have you had a heart attack, stroke, or blockages in your heart or neck arteries?
Are your feet often cold, or is one foot cooler than the other?
Have you noticed less hair on your legs or shiny skin over your shins?
Does your leg pain or numbness improve when you sit down or lean forward?
key_questions.looking_for: Relief with flexion suggests neurogenic claudication, not PAD

key_questions.question: Do you have any back pain, swelling in one leg, or calf tenderness?
key_questions.looking_for: Spinal stenosis or DVT as alternative causes

key_questions.question: For men: any difficulty getting or keeping an erection?
key_questions.looking_for: Erectile dysfunction; indicator of aortoiliac disease

reasoning_points: Exertional cramping in a large muscle group that begins after a predictable distance and resolves within minutes of rest
Risk factors for atherosclerosis, including smoking and diabetes
Diminished or absent pedal pulses with cool skin or trophic changes
No evidence of acute limb ischemia or critical limb ischemia
Neurogenic claudication, DVT, chronic venous insufficiency, and neuropathy considered and excluded

easy: Older adult smoker with classic calf claudication after two blocks
Diminished pedal pulses and no rest pain
medium: Diabetic with noncompressible vessels and painless ulcer or atypical pain; toe-brachial index needed
Coexisting lumbar spinal stenosis with bilateral leg pain that improves with leaning forward
Claudication in hip or thigh from iliac disease rather than calf
hard: Critical limb ischemia presenting with rest pain and gangrene, requiring urgent revascularization
Elderly patient with limited mobility and no classic claudication, found after nonhealing ulcer
Suspected acute limb ischemia superimposed on chronic PAD with sudden worsening
Painless ischemia in neuropathy with medial calcification making ABI falsely normal
